clone_cost.note: our estimate with assumptions visible; not a claim about the team

assumptions: you accept an existing clinical formula rather than fitting your own, so coefficients are copied from a paper
you have users willing to connect real blood panels, since without panels the score is wearable noise
no regulatory clearance is implied; a consumer dashboard, not a diagnostic device
value.estimate: about a week for the pipeline, longer for anything you would defend clinically
value.why: Reading the published PhenoAge formula and applying nine lab values is a day's work; HealthKit and Health Connect auth plus a Gemini schema-constrained PDF pass is another few. The part that does not come free is a labelled corpus to know your parser is right, and any claim about reversing aging.

data_and_models.value: No training of their own: Gemini 1.5 Flash does document parsing under schema constraints, and the clinical model is the published Levine PhenoAge parameterisation over nine biomarkers. Nothing states how the PhenoAge coefficients were sourced or checked, and no validation cohort, sample size or error bar is described for the biological-age output.

how_it_works.value: Marketed as a longevity dashboard: it claims to translate clinical biomarker algorithms into an actionable score, “quantify, gamify, and actively reverse” aging. Built as React Native with NativeWind and Tailwind for the client, interactive 30-day, 90-day and one-year trend graphs. Gemini 1.5 Flash via Google Cloud parses multi-page lab PDFs into validated JSON schemas. The core algorithm is the Levine PhenoAge model: nine biomarkers (albumin, creatinine, glucose, hs-CRP, lymphocyte percentage, mean corpuscular volume, red cell distribution width, alkaline phosphatase, white blood cell count) mapped to a mortality-risk score through a Gompertz distribution. Node.js services on Cloud Run with Firestore for documents and live sync.

how_they_tested.value: The one quantified result - over 95% PDF parsing accuracy - has no denominator: no document count, no provider breakdown, no definition of what counts as correct extraction, and no held-out set. No test suite, repo, or eval harness is linked anywhere on the page, and no clinical or statistical validation is claimed for the age score itself.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Lab PDFs differ by provider (Quest, LabCorp, local clinics) in units and layout, which they addressed with grammar-constrained decoding so the model must emit a strict schema. Wearable HRV and resting heart rate are volatile day to day, so 7-day and 30-day exponentially weighted moving averages smooth the inputs and stop the score from jumping. Recomputing the model while drawing trend graphs pushed them to move the maths into lightweight on-device utility modules.

value.relation: same architecture of trust - a published clinical score presented through a calm UI with an escalation-style recommendation loop - and the same unmeasured gap between a computed index and validated guidance.

opposite end of the same problem: Medvoice closes a loop on an action the patient confirms, while this one opens a recommendation loop with no adherence signal at all. Comparing them shows what a verification step buys.

what_breaks_first.value: Trust in the score, the moment it moves for a reason the user can see is unrelated to their behaviour. A PhenoAge output is dominated by blood chemistry that changes quarterly, while the weekly loop promises movement from sleep and steps, so the dashboard's cadence and the model's sensitivity disagree; the reported parsing accuracy cannot rescue it either, since a single misread unit becomes a wrong age.

what_it_does.value: Passive biometric sync pulls resting heart rate, HRV, VO2 max, sleep architecture and daily steps from HealthKit or Google Health Connect. A multimodal parser reads un-standardised lab PDFs and blood panels (HbA1c, hs-CRP, lipid profile, albumin, alkaline phosphatase) into structured biomarker values. A clock engine computes a biological age and compares it with the chronological baseline. A weekly Longevity Delta loop names the user's biometric bottleneck and returns three targeted lifestyle, protocol or supplement interventions. Monthly Wrapped-style proof cards are generated for sharing.

what_it_is.value: A biological-age dashboard that parses lab PDFs with Gemini into validated schemas, runs the Levine PhenoAge clock over wearable streams, and returns a weekly three-item intervention list.

what_to_steal.value: Force the extraction model into a strict response schema per provider instead of writing per-provider parsers, and keep the raw values alongside the parsed ones; smooth noisy physiological inputs over a short and a long window so a derived score cannot jitter day to day; ship the derived score against a baseline the user already trusts (chronological age) rather than as a bare number.

hazard.note: A biological-age score computed from a mortality model, presented to consumers with weekly supplement and protocol recommendations, and a roadmap that plans to predict how interventions shift the curve. Nothing on the page frames the output as non-medical, and no clinician review, cohort or validation is mentioned for the score its interface is built around.

vitalis-bio.name: Vitalis Bio
verdict_reasons: soundness 0.50 over 64% of the rubric; 0 named unknown(s) remain → publishable with caveats
vitalis-bio.worth_note: Two pieces are worth taking and one is worth doubting. Grammar-constrained decoding for provider-specific PDF layouts is a real technique for any document pipeline, and smoothing volatile wearable inputs with nested EMAs before feeding a scoring model is the unglamorous fix that makes a score stable enough to display. The product itself sits in a crowded longevity-dashboard category whose hardest part - whether the number means anything - is exactly where the page offers a percentage with no denominator.

data_and_models.value: No model trained or fine-tuned: Pydantic-validated deterministic extraction, rule-based history-aware risk scoring, and FAISS retrieval over a locally stored concussion-guideline corpus. The generative model is not presented as the decision-maker, which is the architecturally correct choice for this domain.

how_it_works.value: Full-stack web app: FastAPI service, Streamlit frontend, Pydantic validation of every structured result before display, SQLite history, FAISS retrieval over a local concussion-guideline corpus, deterministic local symptom extraction, history-aware risk scoring, red-flag guardrails, privacy-conscious logging, and offline regression/safety/quality benchmarks. Deployed on Render.

how_they_tested.value: Offline regression, safety and quality benchmarks exist and the page states plainly that they 'demonstrate consistency within our included test cases, not clinical validation'. No case count, split, seed or harness is published, and no test code is linked, so the pass rate is not reproducible by a reader.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Usefulness against safety: no false reassurance, no overstated certainty. Red flags prioritised, escalation made visually prominent, normal progression suppressed when urgent signs appear, recommendations kept conservative, results schema-validated before rendering. Also representing recovery over time rather than as one score.

what_breaks_first.value: The self-graded benchmark: 100% across a case set nobody outside the team defined or counted measures their agreement with themselves, and the page is honest enough to say it is not clinical validation - so a clone inherits the need for a real evaluation with data and a clinician. Second, multi-day history with no persistence story (secure cross-session storage is still on the roadmap).

what_it_does.value: Free-text symptom description plus optional guided questions, a structured symptom summary, a conservative risk assessment, a five-stage recovery plan, evidence supporting the guidance, multi-day trend view (improving / stable / worsening), and a caregiver or clinician handoff summary. Urgent warning signs replace normal advice with escalation.

what_it_is.value: A daily concussion check-in that extracts symptoms deterministically, scores risk against recovery history, and escalates red flags before it offers any advice.

what_to_steal.value: Escalation precedence: compute the red-flag rules first and *suppress* the normal path when they fire, rather than letting a friendly assistant narrate its way past a warning sign. Pair it with schema validation of every structured result before it renders, and hand the professional a summary artifact rather than a chat transcript.

hazard.note: Risk assessment on a medical condition. The team disclaims diagnosis, states the benchmarks are not clinical validation, and keeps recommendations conservative; that is better hygiene than most of the corpus, not permission to run it on real patients without oversight.

neuroguard-ai-adaptiveconcussionrecovery.worth_note: The architecture is the contribution: deterministic extraction, rule-based history-aware scoring, retrieval over a guideline corpus, and escalation that pre-empts advice - with the generative model kept out of the decision path. That is the correct shape for software that touches a regulated outcome, and it is rare to see it chosen deliberately at hackathon scale.
